- If sentiment is consistently positive or neutral in recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast slope or cap upward momentum.
- If sentiment turns negative or shows strong bearish signals (e.g., -0.20 or below), model often fails to adjust downward; increase downward bias or introduce early correction.
- After sharp price spikes (e.g., >10% from prior day), model frequently overshoots and fails to correct; apply lagged mean reversion or reduce forecast slope post-spike.
- When sentiment is flat or zero (e.g., 0.00), model often overfits recent trends; apply smoothing or reduce forecast volatility.
- If true outcome shows strong mean reversion (e.g., 3–5 consecutive days below 80), model tends to ignore it; adjust forecast to align with recent low volatility or downward drift.
- For 30-day forecasts, model often overestimates early in the horizon; consider anchoring to 10–15 day moving average or sentiment-weighted average for first 5–7 days.
- If sentiment history shows repeated negative sentiment (e.g., 3+ consecutive 0.00 or negative), model tends to underreact; apply a downward bias multiplier (e.g., 0.85–0.90) to forecast.
